title: Two mutable views of one buffer

prereqs.why: Two exclusive borrows of one Vec is the thing the compiler forbids, and this is the exercise that runs into it.
Both halves are slices of the same buffer, which is why they cannot be taken independently.
Nothing is moved and nothing is copied: the function borrows the caller’s buffer and rearranges it in place.

statement:
Read `n`, then `n` integers.

If `n` is odd, print

```
odd
```

and stop. Otherwise treat the first half and the second half as two
sequences of the same length, and for each position `i`, if
`left[i] > right[i]`, **swap** the two values. Then print:

```
swaps <how many swaps were made>
left <the first half after the swaps>
right <the second half after the swaps>
```

Both value lines are printed even when `n` is 0, with nothing after the
label.

### The sample

```
6
5 1 9 2 7 3
```

```
swaps 2
left 2 1 3
right 5 7 9
```

Position `i` of the left half is paired with position `i` of the right
half, so the pairs are `5` with `2`, `1` with `7`, and `9` with `3`.
Two of the three are out of order.

### The point of the exercise

Write

```rust
fn settle(v: &mut [i64]) -> usize
```

so that it rearranges the caller's buffer in place — no copy of either
half, no second `Vec`.

That is harder than it sounds, because the two halves are parts of one
slice and taking a mutable borrow of each is exactly what the borrow
checker forbids:

```rust
let left  = &mut v[..mid];
let right = &mut v[mid..];   // error: cannot borrow `*v` as mutable more than once
```

There is a method on slices that does it, and the whole reason it
exists is this situation.
hints: The compiler is right to refuse the two separate borrows: it cannot tell from `&mut v[..mid]` and `&mut v[mid..]` that the two ranges do not overlap, and if they did you would have two exclusive references to one element.
Search the slice documentation for the method that returns a **pair**. One call, one borrow going in, two non-overlapping mutable slices coming out.

`let (left, right) = v.split_at_mut(mid);` is the line. It takes `&mut self`, consumes that one borrow, and hands back two — which is sound precisely because the method guarantees the halves do not overlap.
To swap two elements that live in different slices, `std::mem::swap(&mut left[i], &mut right[i])` is the general tool. (Within one slice, `v.swap(i, j)` does it without the two borrows.)
